summary: Describes how S/MIME version 2 uses certificates to create and validate keys, so mail clients can check who a signature or encryption key belongs to. It is an informational memo and is now historic.

eli5.summary: Like an ID card for a secret code, showing the code really belongs to the person who says it does. This memo explains how email programs use those ID cards.

questions: what is s/mime version 2 certificate handling
what must an s/mime certificate contain
subtitle: How S/MIME version 2 mail programs create, check and manage X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: To trust the key behind a signed or encrypted S/MIME message, an agent has to certify that the key is valid and really belongs to the sender.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets rules on top of PKCS #7: which X.509 certificate and CRL features agents must support, how Internet mail addresses go into certificates, how chains are validated, and how certification requests are made.
tldr.outcome: The memo is informational, historical material published for the public record, and is not an IETF standard. It is now Historic.

today: RFC 2312 is Informational and Historic, and its own text calls it historical material, not an IETF standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Overview and Scope
sections.content:
S/MIME provides a way to send and receive secure MIME messages. To validate the keys of a message, an S/MIME agent must be able to certify that the key is valid. This memo describes the mechanisms S/MIME uses to create and validate keys using certificates.

It is compatible with PKCS #7 and inherits the architectures for certificate-based key management that PKCS #7 supports. Agents must also follow parts of PKCS #1, PKCS #7 and PKCS #10. The memo warns that it is historical material published for the public record. The word "standard" in it means a standard for adopters of S/MIME version 2, not an IETF standard.
sections.eli5: Before you trust a secret code, you need proof it belongs to the right person. This memo explains how email programs get that proof.

sections.title: Certificate and CRL Requirements
sections.content:
Receiving agents MUST support X.509 v1 and v3 certificates and the certificate revocation list (CRL) format from the key management profile. Agents MUST NOT use PKCS #6 extended certificates, which were not in widespread use. Receiving agents MUST handle any number of certificates in any order, and MUST support chaining by distinguished name.

Sending agents SHOULD include the user's certificates and the issuer certificates, including at least one chain up to, but not including, a CA the recipient may trust. This can be left out within groups that already share certificates some other way. Receiving agents SHOULD NOT simply trust any self-signed certificate as a CA.

CRLs received in messages MUST be recognized and used when verifying signatures and paths, and SHOULD be stored. Agents SHOULD check the CRL nextUpdate field, but what to do about an old CRL is a local decision.
sections.eli5: Mail programs must be able to read the common kinds of ID cards and the lists of cancelled ones. They should also be careful not to trust an ID card that vouches only for itself.

sections.title: Names in Certificates
sections.content:
X.509 certificates name their subject and issuer with X.500 distinguished names, but real X.500 directories were slow to spread. Internet mail addresses are what people actually use. S/MIME therefore keeps X.509 and distinguished names and tailors the content to mail.

End-entity certificates MUST contain an Internet mail address (an RFC 822 addr-spec), and receiving agents MUST recognize it in subjectAltName and in the distinguished name. Receiving agents MUST check that the From header address matches an address in the signer's certificate, and MUST do some explicit alternate processing if not, which may be to reject the message. Agents must parse name attributes such as CountryName, CommonName, Organization and EmailAddress.
sections.eli5: People know each other by email address, so the ID card has to include one. If the "From" address on the letter does not match the ID card, the program must not just ignore it.

sections.title: Retrieving and Validating Certificates
sections.content:
Agents need a way to retrieve certificates, for example X.500, or possibly the DNS, both of which the memo describes as under consideration. At a minimum, a user agent could send a message asking a recipient to reply with a signed message holding their certificate. Agents SHOULD let users store certificates, much like an address book, and import and export them as PKCS #7 certs-only messages.

Certificate, CRL and chain validation MUST be done when verifying a signature and when creating a digital envelope for a recipient. Receiving agents MUST verify certificate signatures made with md5WithRSAEncryption and sha-1WithRSAEncryption, with key sizes from 512 bits to 2048 bits, and SHOULD verify md2WithRSAEncryption. Agents MUST handle the v3 Basic Constraints and Key Usage extensions, authorityKeyID, subjectKeyID and subjectAltNames in end-user certificates. Other critical extensions SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.eli5: The program should keep a little address book of ID cards, check each card and the cancelled-card list every time, and use only well-known kinds of checks.

sections.title: Keys and Certification Requests
sections.content:
An S/MIME agent or related tool MUST be able to generate a certification request from a public key and name information, using PKCS #10. There SHOULD NOT be several valid certificates for one key pair bound to different distinguished names, since an attacker could swap one for another undetected. A user who wants a new name should generate a new key pair or first revoke the old certificates.

Requests MUST include a valid Internet mail address, and CAs MUST check it against the From header. RSA keys SHOULD be identified with rsaEncryption and requests signed with sha-1WithRSAEncryption, and MUST NOT be signed with md2WithRSAEncryption. A CA answers with a degenerate PKCS #7 SignedData message that has no signers and carries the certificate, plus ideally the chain and CRLs.
sections.eli5: To get an ID card you send an application with your email address. The card issuer sends back your card in a special envelope with the cards of the people who vouch for them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
S/MIME agents face every issue of a cryptographic application, including protecting the private key, preventing attacks, and avoiding mistakes such as encrypting for the wrong recipient. The RFC says that when a certificate cannot be shown to be valid and tied to the message, software should take immediate and noticeable steps to inform the user.

It lists places where checking can fail: no certificate address matches the sender, no chain leads to a trusted CA, a CRL cannot be checked, is invalid or has expired, or the certificate is expired or revoked.
sections.eli5: If an ID card looks fake, expired or cancelled, the program has to tell you loudly and not quietly carry on.
